{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Idea A has a business payer, and at least one competitor lists a price: Since.dev's Studio tier at $149/mo for 15 repos, from a direct fetch. Idea B has no competitor charging anything. Every listed alternative is free or donation-supported.",
    "Idea B's strongest market signal is negative. Fakespot was free, well funded and well distributed, and it shut down in July 2025. The brief itself reads this as evidence the category struggles to make money even at scale.",
    "Idea A's demand quotes describe concrete production failures with business cost: user complaints, a Stripe payload change breaking billing. Idea B's quotes are general frustration, and one ('downright immoral') is backlash against the product itself.",
    "Idea A's pipeline (watch, diff, match call sites, draft fix, open PR) suits one person running AI agents. Several near-solo teams have reportedly shipped working MVPs in weeks, so it can be built within 90 days.",
    "Idea A has serious risks: a crowded field, free open-source engines, and the trust and SOC 2 barrier to getting PR access to customer code. These threaten how fast it can grow and how much it can charge. Idea B's risks threaten whether anyone will pay at all, and a paying customer within 90 days is the actual goal."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea B's price hypothesis of ~$3-5/month is borrowed from GPTZero's $10-15/month individual tier, cited through a third-party aggregator. GPTZero is a different product category with different buyers. The '$4.99/month typical extension subscription' figure carries no source. The brief admits no one in the category charges today, so B has no direct evidence that any reader will pay.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate. Idea A's pricing evidence is thinner than it looks. Nalvis's $14/mo tier is pre-launch/waitlist, Since.dev's Pro price is undisclosed, and neither brief shows that any customer actually pays these prices. Two of A's three demand quotes come from builders' 'how I built a fix' posts, which are partly promotional. The trust and security-review barrier could push a first paying customer past 90 days. Still, B has zero evidence of willingness to pay, while A has at least one live paid price in a business market. That gap is enough to separate them."
}
